h: Stockton climbing, plus a Teesside day out
p: Here's the beauty of an indoor climbing centre on Teesside: it doesn't matter if it's blowing a gale off the North Sea or drizzling all afternoon, the walls are ready and waiting. Still, a little planning makes the day far smoother.

Every climber will need a participation form completing, with a parent or guardian signing for under-18s. Fill it in online before you go, and check-in will be quick. Have a look at the age guidance when you book, too, as there's usually a minimum age for climbers and supervision rules for younger children. Allow a couple of hours for the full visit, including arrival, harness fitting and the safety briefing.

On the walls, pace yourselves. Start low and easy, build up to the race walls, and leave the big jumps until last. Climb with your legs rather than your arms and you'll get through far more of the challenges before the burn kicks in. Eat light, bring water and wear trainers.

Afterwards, the Tees Barrage, just downstream from the town centre, is home to the Tees Barrage International White Water Centre, where you can watch rafters and kayakers tackling the rapids, or have a go yourself if you book. The Infinity Bridge, a striking footbridge over the Tees, looks especially good lit up after dark. RSPB Saltholme, over towards Seal Sands, is a fantastic wetland reserve for spotting birds, and Middlesbrough's Captain Cook Birthplace Museum in Stewart Park is a short drive away for a bit of history.
